blocks.text: The British locked Subhas Chandra Bose inside his own home. Guards at the gate, CID agents on the street, but months later his voice suddenly crackled over the radio from Berlin telling India to rise up. >> But whether we survive or not, we are confident that India shall be free. >> For 10 days the British had been guarding an empty room completely unaware their most dangerous prisoner was already gone. The last Indian to humiliate an empire like this was Chhatrapati Shivaji

Maharaj slipping out of Aurangzeb's grip. This is the story of how Bose beat the British surveillance state, crossed the world at war, and raised an army for India's freedom. >> The British had jailed Bose for leading a protest, and when he nearly starved himself to death in prison, they let him out but locked him inside his home. Behind that door he was  planning his escape, but how do you disappear when the whole country knows your face?

So for almost a month he grew a beard. A beard changed how he looked, but if he spoke even one word people would recognize his voice and know exactly who he was. >>  >> His voice was just as famous as his face. One sentence at a checkpoint, it was over. So he became Muhammad Ziauddin, a Pathan insurance agent in a baggy trousers and heavy  coat. A man who could not hear and could not speak. Months earlier his family  had quietly obtained the police files on him. The dossier naming the men assigned

to watch the house. Bose knew who was outside. He knew their shifts. He knew which one to slip past.  On the night of 16th January 1941, a cousin kept eyes on the agents at the gate. Bose walked out of his house, climbed into back of a car, and let his nephew Sisir drive him straight past the men paid to stop him. The British had no idea that Bose had escaped right under their noses. Every checkpoint was a trap. If even one guard knew his face, it was over. He would be arrested and

escape would end before it begin. So, he moved at night. First, he took a train northwest all the way to Peshawar, close to the edge of British India. That was the easy part. The hard part was the border. Past the Peshawar, the road ran into tribal lands, a stretch of mountains and open country where British spies watched every traveler. He crossed those lands on foot and by car and reached Kabul, the capital of Afghanistan. But Kabul was not safe. It was full of enemies. The British agents

worked the streets. Italian and German contacts watched him, too. Everyone wanted to know who this quiet Pathan man really was. For weeks, he hid in the city waiting for one door to open. Then it did. He got secret help from the Italians. Took on a new fake name and slipped out by car towards the north. He crossed into Soviet Union, reached  Moscow. >> But Stalin didn't trust the Indian nationalist. He feared that Bose might be a British agent. >> And from there, he finally boarded a

plane to Berlin. And here's the strange part. For weeks, British agents kept watching his room still believing he was inside. When they finally checked the room and found it empty, panic reached the top of British government. They officially theorized that his disappearance might not be a planned escape, but an aberration suggesting he wandered off to become a sannyasi because his horoscope predicted he would become one in his 46th year. By this time, Bose had stopped believing India would be freed by non-violence. It

would have to be taken by force. And to take it, he needed an army, which meant he needed a sponsor. And the only powers willing to arm Indians against British were the ones already at war with Britain. But what could a hunted fugitive offer a world at war? A plan to dismantle British Empire from within. Bose turned to Berlin offering the Nazi leadership propaganda, armed uprising and an Indian legion in exchange for support. It took him over a year to get to the meeting.

>> Subhas Chandra Bose certainly knew about the dark  side of Nazi ideology. And I think he was making some kind of a Faustian bargain, you know, in order to end what  he saw as the scourge of British rule in India. >> While he waited, he built a small army of Indian prisoner of wars and started a radio station to reach India. >> Bose wanted to reach  the 2 million Indian volunteers of the British Indian Army. These men were the bedrock of the

British  Raj. >> He believed that Britain's Indian Army was the ultimate instrument  of colonial control, not just in India, but in the British Empire worldwide. And therefore,  he set out to undermine the loyalty of Indian soldiers to the King Emperor. >> Then Hitler finally  saw him and gave him a lecture. There was no sense of declaring Indian independence, he explained, until Britain had >>  >> actually been beaten. Besides, German tanks were thousands of miles from India. His advice was simple, go east,

ask the Japanese. Bose had crossed the continent to be told to leave. He turned to the translator, "Please tell His Excellency that I have been in politics all my life. I don't need advice from anyone." The translator hesitated. By 1943, realizing that Germany was in war with Russia and could no longer aid India, he knew he had to reach Asia. With the Japanese were dismantling the British Empire. But reaching Asia meant crossing an ocean the allies controlled. The British had already started to hunt

him. What came next was a journey almost no one believed a politician could risk his life. Bose was about to attempt the most dangerous journey of his life. Waters crawling with U-boat hunters and Allied destroyers hunting anything that moved. >> He boarded the German submarine U-180 and quietly slipped away leaving behind his wife and daughter. To avoid being detected by British destroyers in the English Channel,

Bose's U-boat was heading for the icy waters north  of Scotland. >> Now, he has to travel from Germany to a submarine waiting for him in Indian Ocean. In February 1943, Bose climbed aboard the German submarine spending nearly 90 days inside a suffocating steel tube as it dodged Allied depth charges around the Cape of Good Hope. But, the most dangerous moment was still to come. The British were hunting him the whole way. Ever since he vanished from Calcutta, British intelligence had been searching for him. They knew he was

alive. His own broadcast on Berlin radio had made sure of that. They just don't know where he was. So, they watched the ports. They watched the coast. And the Royal Navy hunted every enemy submarine it could find in these waters. If they caught this one U-boat, they caught Bose. One depth charge in the right spot and the whole story ended at the bottom of the ocean. Then off the coast of Madagascar, the German submarine surfaced in the open ocean and waited. A Japanese submarine was doing the same.

In the pitch dark open sea, two enemies of Britain were about to attempt something never done in the war, moving a passenger from one submarine to the another mid-ocean with destroyers hunting nearby. There was no dock, no harbor. Two enemy submarines sat exposed on the surface of the Indian Ocean while one man climbed into a rubber raft and rode between them. In the middle of the night in a heavy swell, the handoff worked. From that submarine, Bose pushed on across the last stretch of the ocean and

by the May, he reached Tokyo. Where he secured the backing of Japanese Prime Minister Tojo. But what did Japan actually want from him? He wouldn't find the real answer for another year and when he did, it almost destroyed everything he had built. Reaching Singapore by July, Rash Behari Bose handed him the leadership of Indian Independence  League. >> Bose now proceeded to Singapore. He received a hero's welcome by thousands of Indian volunteers, members

of the Indian National Army under Japanese command. >> The leadership was his, or so it looked, but there was nothing left to lead because Bose wasn't stepping into a united movement. An Indian National Army already existed and it had spent the previous year tearing itself apart. The men who had built it were convinced the Japanese saw them as convenience rather than an ally. Useful while the war was going well and disposable afterwards.

Its founder refused to hand over control of his soldiers and was arrested for it. Tokyo refused to put Indian independence in writing. To the soldiers, it looked like they were just trading British masters for Japanese ones. That was the inheritance. Soldiers who had watched their own commander taken away. An ally that would not commit to the thing they were fighting for and a promise to march on Delhi. How do you build an army that turned on itself? The way he fixed it is the reason people  started calling him Netaji. First, he negotiated

with the Japanese to have INA recognized as an allied army rather than a puppet force, ensuring it fought with far greater political and military autonomy. But an army needs soldiers, and he had promised a force big enough to take India. Where would the rest of them come from? He did something no army in the world was doing at  that time. He shattered traditional military norms by raising the Rani of Jhansi Regiment, an all-female combat unit with rifles. But his biggest achievement was expanding

INA beyond prisoner of wars. Through a campaign of total mobilization, he turned to huge and prosperous Indian diaspora scattered across Southeast Asia and recruited civilians until they made up nearly 40% of the force. Most remarkably, he forged a common identity that transcended religion, region, and caste.  Back in India, the Congress was struggling to eradicate communal divides for years. The INA united Hindus, Muslims, and Sikhs under a single cause within months. He gave

that shared cause a single war cry that every soldier could shout on a march. Chalo Delhi. And then he did one thing which would help his army even after he died. In October 1943 in Singapore, Bose proclaimed a government of his own, the Provisional Government of Free India. It had a cabinet, a currency, a bank, and a declaration of war on Britain. Several Axis states recognized it. For the first time, Bose was no longer asking stronger

power to sponsor his cause. He had manufactured his own legitimacy. It was a government with almost no territory, but on paper, it was a real state. And that one piece of paper was about to win him something no Indian leader had held in living memory. Japan formally ceded nominal administration of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands to Bose's new government. Japan functioned not as an ally, but as a silent, calculative adviser, keeping all the real military

authority for itself. It had never wanted a free India. It wanted a propaganda asset and a buffer force for its own campaign. In early 1944, thousands of INA soldiers marched with Japanese towards northeast India crying  "Chalo Delhi". >> The Japanese expected an easy victory, just like in 1942. But this time, the British were ahead of the game.

>> For Bose, this was not really about capturing Delhi. He wanted to prove one thing, that Indians would actually stand up and fight, even if it cost him everything. They advanced to capture Manipur, but the Japanese commanders made critical strategic errors. Instead of striking the nearest British railhead and supply base in eastern Assam, they dug in for long siege, exactly what an undersupplied army could least afford. The INA had carried almost no supplies of its own. The entire plan depended on British breaking fast, so Bose's men could capture their food stores and eat

off the enemy. Neither came. The British held, dug in on high ground, and let the mountains and weather do the rest. As INA pushed deeper, severe supply shortages emerged. They were marching into regions plagued by extreme cold and malaria, with only one blanket each and no mosquito nets. Starving and short of weapons, the INA fought its way to the outskirts of Imphal. They could see it. After everything, the ocean crossing, the broken army rebuilt from nothing, the march through mountains, and the

town they had come for was finally within reach. An Indian army was standing on the edge of Indian soil, and back home, the British would spend enormous effort making sure no one ever heard about it. This was as close as the dream of marching on Delhi could ever come. But they had gone in with almost nothing, five loads of ammunition and no artillery to answer the British guns. As the British reinforced the positions, an early monsoon flooded the jungle and cut off INA's supply lines. The Japanese

were not being cruel for its own sake. They were losing badly to the Americans across the Pacific. A drowning army saves itself first. So they pulled the air cover east and held to what they had left. And then food ran out. Starving, the men boiled jungle grass to fill their stomachs. Malaria burned through the camps. Leeches did the rest. Thousands died in the mud, not from British bullets, but from hunger and disease. Subhas Chandra Bose personally met the soldiers, greeting everyone and boosting their morale. He traveled to

the base hospital to personally visit 2,000 wounded soldiers being cared by his Rani Jhansi Regiment. He expanded his army's strength to 50,000 men. However, the British were organizing a massive The INA was walking into a battle it could not win, but Netaji's objective was never a military victory. He was chasing an outcome that would only reveal itself in the years to come. >> The Japanese generals and officers  had a lot of respect for Bose. And some of them said to me privately,

"There is no person in the war >>  >> who more fully fit the ideal of a samurai than Subhas Chandra Bose." >> So what does Bose do when his army starts to lose? He does the opposite of what any general would do. He goes straight towards the fighting. And this was one of the reason people started calling him Netaji. As the front lines collapsed, Bose drove towards the advancing British artillery. When he was asked, "Why risk everything for a visit

to doomed outpost?" he said, "England has not yet produced the bomb that can kill Subhas Chandra Bose." When Burma fell, Bose refused to evacuate until female combat unit, the Rani Jhansi Regiment, was safe first. Then he faced a final grueling trek. 3:00 in the morning, the Sittang River, vehicles burning behind him so British couldn't use them. Netaji walked because his men were walking. 21 days later, he emerged in Bangkok shattered. His army and base were gone. While he was retreating, the two governments he had risked everything

for were collapsing behind him. Within months, both had ceased to exist. Bose received the news that Japan had surrendered. >> The end of the worst war in human history. >> He turned to his aides and said, "So that is that. Now, what next?" The answer was Soviets. Germany was lost. Japan had just surrendered and exactly one great power left that was not British Empire. He decided to go to them. The Soviets and the British had

just fought on the same side against Germany, but they had been imperial enemies for a century. Bose gambled that Moscow might still be willing to listen. The route north through Manchuria. He was about to ask the same question for a third foreign government. Whether the Soviets would have taken him, no one knows. On the eve of the flight, he wrote a message to his secretary, Major Bhaskar Menon, "I'm writing all this to you on the eve of a long journey by air and who knows, an accident might overtake me." His last words to his comrades were, "Well, Jai Hind. I will

meet you later." From here, the official story goes something like this. On 18th of August, 1945, his overloaded bomber came down shortly after takeoff. Bose sustained severe burns and he died that night. >> Bose died as a result of severe burns. >> He was cremated in Taipei and his surviving passenger, Habib ur Rahman, carried his ashes to Tokyo to the Renkoji Temple, but the story did not stop when Bose did.

Netaji was dead. So, how did a man who lost end up winning? Here's the answer. Britain was broke after World War II, but money wasn't the thing they couldn't fix. The loyalty they ruled dependent on was gone. When the British put captured INA officers on trial in Delhi, the spectacle backfired. It brought to light wartime censorship had buried, that an Indian liberation army had actually reached Indian soil to fight the British Raj. Protest erupted across the country, and the British cracked down hard. In Feb 1946, fueled by anti-British

sentiment and blatant racism of British commanders, the breaking point arrived. Thousands of soldiers across dozens of ships in Royal Indian Navy refused to take orders. They raised the flag of the freedom movement and held out for days. The British rule in India sat on one simple fact, Indian soldiers obeyed British officers. That fact was now dead. The man who later admitted why Britain left was not an Indian. It was Britain's own Prime Minister, Clement Attlee, the man who signed India away.

Years later, when asked what really pushed Britain out, and whether it was Gandhi's non-violence, he pointed to one name instead, Subhas Chandra Bose and his INA, which leaves one question open and never quite closed. His ashes are still sitting in Tokyo 80 years later. No Indian government brought them home, and no Indian government has been willing to say they are his. Because the official story of that plane crash, the one we just told you, was never actually satisfied anyone. And what really happened on 18th August of 1945 is a
mystery we are going to open in the next part.
